item.title: Fixing JavaFX Runtime Components Missing Error with JDK 11+
item.description:
“Fixing JavaFX Runtime Components Missing Error with JDK 11+”

When upgrading to Java Development Kit (JDK) 11 or later, developers often encounter the persistent error: “JavaFX runtime components are missing, and are required to run this application.” This arises because, unlike previous Java versions, JavaFX is no longer bundled directly within the JDK. Instead, it needs to be explicitly included as a separate dependency. This post delves into the various methods to resolve this issue, whether you’re working with standard JavaFX projects, Maven, or Gradle.

item.title: JavaFX: How to Get Node Dimensions Before Scene is Visible
item.description:
“JavaFX: How to Get Node Dimensions Before Scene is Visible”

When developing JavaFX applications, a frequent requirement arises: calculating the precise pixel dimensions (width and height) of a UI element, such as a Button or Label, before the Stage has been shown or fully rendered. Normally, JavaFX manages layout computations asynchronously during its internal “pulse” cycle, resulting in calls to getWidth() or getHeight() returning zero before this cycle completes.

How can a developer force the necessary styling and layout passes to obtain accurate measurements?

item.title: JavaFX: Safely Updating UI from Background Threads
item.description:
“JavaFX: Safely Updating UI from Background Threads”

When developing JavaFX applications that involve background tasks, such as database queries or network requests, it’s crucial to adhere to specific threading rules to maintain UI responsiveness and prevent runtime errors. The most common issue encountered is the IllegalStateException: Not on FX application thread, which arises when attempting to modify the JavaFX scene graph from a thread other than the dedicated JavaFX Application Thread.

item.title: Resolving JavaFX IllegalAccessError with Java Module System
item.description:
“Resolving JavaFX IllegalAccessError with Java Module System”

How do you correct a java.lang.IllegalAccessError when loading JavaFX media components, specifically when the error points to an unnamed module attempting to access an exported class within the javafx.graphics module?

The observed error typically looks like this:

java.lang.IllegalAccessError: class com.sun.media.jfxmediaimpl.NativeMediaManager (in unnamed module @0x4d7be377) cannot access class com.sun.glass.utils.NativeLibLoader (in module javafx.graphics) because module javafx.graphics does not export com.sun.glass.utils to unnamed module @0x4d7be377

Deep Dive into the Module Problem

This error signifies that a class belonging to the unnamed module (classes loaded from the classpath) is trying to reflectively access an internal class within the named module javafx.graphics. The named module explicitly restricts this access via qualified exports or opens directives, which are only respected when the accessing code is also properly recognized as a module or part of the module system’s awareness.

item.title: JavaFX FXML Static Field Injection & Method Errors: Solutions Explained
item.description:
“JavaFX FXML Static Field Injection & Method Errors: Solutions Explained”

It appears you’re encountering problems with static fields or methods annotated with @FXML when using JavaFX 8. This behavior, while seemingly functional in older versions like JavaFX 2.2, is not officially supported and can lead to javafx.fxml.LoadException errors, particularly with onAction event handlers.

The core issue stems from how FXMLLoader operates. When you load an FXML file, FXMLLoader instantiates a new controller for each load operation. Instance fields within this controller are then injected with the corresponding UI elements defined in the FXML. Making these fields static breaks this instance-specific injection. If you were to load the same FXML multiple times to display different instances of your UI, static fields would all point to the same single instance, making it impossible to differentiate between the controls of each UI instance.

item.title: JavaFX Fat Jar Issues and Modern Distribution Alternatives
item.description:
“JavaFX Fat Jar Issues and Modern Distribution Alternatives”

When building JavaFX applications, particularly those intended for wider distribution, packaging them into a single “fat” or “uber” jar is a common desire. However, this approach can lead to specific errors, especially with JavaFX versions like 11 and later, and brings forth modern alternatives for more robust application distribution.

Why Do Fat/Uber Jars Fail with JavaFX 11+?

The core of the problem lies in how JavaFX, since version 11, is distributed as a set of modular JAR files. The JavaFX runtime specifically expects these modules to be present and loaded correctly within the module path. When you create a fat jar, you are essentially bypassing the module path and placing all classes onto the classpath.

item.title: JavaFX MVC: Separating Concerns for Robust Applications
item.description:
“JavaFX MVC: Separating Concerns for Robust Applications”

When developing JavaFX applications, structuring your code according to design patterns like Model-View-Controller (MVC) is crucial for maintainability and scalability. A common point of discussion within MVC implementation, especially in JavaFX, revolves around the precise roles of the Model and the Controller, particularly concerning data loading and the management of data structures like ObservableList.

In a web application context, “MVC” can differ slightly from its interpretation in a desktop application due to the inherent request-response cycle of the web. This exploration focuses on a typical thick-client JavaFX application structure.
